C004.subject: Raising the minimum wage in high employer concentration labor markets
C004.object: compression of wage differentials between low-skilled and mid-skilled workers
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in high employer concentration labor markets compression of wage differentials between low-skilled and mid-skilled workers]

[PATH:empirical] Difference-in-differences analysis of minimum wage increases in U.S. counties with high employer concentration (e.g., Herfindahl-Hirschman Index > 2500) using matched employer-employee panel data from the Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics (LEHD) database, focusing on wage compression between low-skilled (bottom quartile) and mid-skilled (median) workers within the same firm. — Directly tests the hypothesis by exploiting exogenous variation in minimum wage laws across local labor markets with high concentration, measuring within-firm wage differentials post-policy change. LEHD data provides fine-grained wage and skill proxies.

[PATH:theoretical] Monopsony wage-setting models with heterogeneous labor and endogenous firm-level wage structures, specifically extending the Burdett-Mortensen equilibrium search model to include a binding minimum wage and employer concentration. Simulate the effect on within-firm wage dispersion between low- and mid-skilled workers under low labor demand elasticity. — Clarifies the causal mechanism: if firms have monopsony power, a minimum wage can compress internal wage hierarchies by raising the floor while mid-skilled wages adjust less. Simulations can identify conditions (e.g., concentration level, elasticity) under which the hypothesis holds or fails.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing empirical studies on minimum wage effects on wage inequality, stratified by measures of employer concentration (e.g., industry-level concentration indices) and skill groups. Focus on studies from advanced economies post-2000 with low labor mobility (e.g., Germany, Japan). — Synthesizes available evidence to assess the robustness and generalizability of the hypothesized effect across different concentration contexts. A meta-regression can test whether concentration moderates the compression effect, providing confirmatory or refutatory evidence.

scope.domain: labor markets with high employer concentration and low labor demand elasticity

qualifier.geographic: advanced economies with low labor mobility

C005.subject: Raising the minimum wage in high employer concentration labor markets
C005.predicate: reduces employment opportunities for low-skilled workers
C005.object: monopsony power causing employers to cut jobs to offset increased labor costs
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in high employer concentration labor markets monopsony power causing employers to cut jobs to offset increased labor costs]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies of minimum wage changes in U.S. counties with high versus low employer concentration, using data from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) and the Census Bureau's Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics (LEHD) program. — Compares employment outcomes for low-skilled workers in concentrated labor markets before and after minimum wage increases, directly testing whether monopsony power leads to job cuts.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of monopsonistic competition in labor markets, particularly the work of Alan Manning (e.g., 'Monopsony in Motion') and subsequent extensions incorporating minimum wage effects under low demand elasticity. — Provides a formal framework to predict when minimum wage hikes reduce employment versus when they may increase it, clarifying the conditions under which the hypothesis holds.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analyses of minimum wage employment effects stratified by market concentration, such as those by Doucouliagos and Stanley (2009) or more recent updates using Bayesian model averaging. — Synthesizes existing empirical evidence across multiple studies to assess whether the employment-reducing effect is systematically stronger in high-concentration labor markets, addressing the disputed status.

C006.subject: Raising the minimum wage in high employer concentration labor markets
C006.predicate: reduces net earnings for low-skilled workers by less than predicted when firms exercise monopsony power through non-wage margin adjustments
C006.object: employers offset wage increases by reducing non-wage compensation and intensifying work schedules, dampening employment losses
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in high employer concentration labor markets employers offset wage increases by reducing non-wage compensation and intensifying work schedules, dampening employment losses]

[PATH:empirical] Analysis of matched employer-employee data from U.S. Census Bureau's Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics (LEHD) program, focusing on retail and fast-food industries in high-concentration metropolitan areas, to measure changes in non-wage compensation (e.g., health benefits, paid leave) and work schedules (e.g., hours per week, irregular scheduling) following minimum wage increases. — Directly tests the hypothesis by quantifying non-wage margin adjustments and their impact on net earnings and employment, using high-frequency, granular data on employer concentration and labor outcomes.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental or quasi-experimental studies of minimum wage hikes in local labor markets with varying employer concentration, such as those using border discontinuity designs (e.g., comparing contiguous counties with different minimum wage levels) and incorporating measures of monopsony power (e.g., Herfindahl-Hirschman Index of employer concentration). — Provides causal evidence on whether high-concentration markets exhibit smaller employment losses and greater non-wage adjustments, directly addressing the core claim about dampened employment effects.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of monopsonistic competition with endogenous non-wage margins (e.g., Burdett-Mortensen search models extended to include fringe benefits and effort), calibrated to U.S. labor market data from the post-2000 period. — Formalizes the mechanisms linking minimum wage increases to non-wage compensation and work intensity, offering testable predictions and identifying conditions under which the hypothesis holds or fails, thereby guiding empirical design.

scope.domain: labor markets with high employer concentration and high labor demand elasticity, where firms can adjust non-wage margins

qualifier.temporal: post-2000 period of rising employer concentration and labor market deregulation
qualifier.geographic: U.S. local labor markets with high employer concentration, such as retail and fast-food industries in metropolitan areas

C007.subject: Raising the minimum wage in high employer concentration labor markets
C007.predicate: increases net earnings for low-skilled workers
C007.object: wage gains outweighing employment reductions in inelastic labor markets
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in high employer concentration labor markets wage gains outweighing employment reductions in inelastic labor markets]

[PATH:empirical] Card and Krueger (1994) minimum wage study replication with modern employer concentration measures (e.g., HHI from Census Longitudinal Business Database) — Re-analyzing the classic New Jersey-Pennsylvania fast-food minimum wage experiment using county-level employer concentration indices and current labor demand elasticity estimates would directly test whether wage gains exceed employment losses in high-concentration, inelastic markets.

[PATH:empirical] Azar, Marinescu, and Steinbaum (2017) on labor market concentration and wages, extended with minimum wage variation — This literature uses online job posting data to measure employer concentration. Extending their analysis to exploit state-level minimum wage changes post-2000 would isolate whether workers in concentrated markets experience net earnings gains despite potential employment reductions.

[PATH:theoretical] Monopsony search models with heterogeneous firms and minimum wage (e.g., Manning 2003; Bhaskar, Manning, To 2002) — These models predict that in monopsonistic markets with low labor demand elasticity, a moderate minimum wage can increase employment and earnings. Calibrating such models to US post-2000 data would provide theoretical confirmation or refutation of the hypothesis under various concentration scenarios.

scope.domain: labor markets with high employer concentration and low labor demand elasticity
